Here's Altair code for creating various visualizations of the Seattle weather dataset:

```python
import altair as alt
from vega_datasets import data

# Load the Seattle weather dataset
seattle_weather = data.seattle_weather()

# 1. Basic line chart showing temperature over time
temp_chart = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_line().encode(
    x='date:T',
    y='temp_max:Q',
    tooltip=['date:T', 'temp_max:Q', 'temp_min:Q']
).properties(
    width=600,
    height=300,
    title='Seattle Maximum Temperature Over Time'
)

# 2. Area chart showing temperature range
temp_range = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_area(opacity=0.3).encode(
    x='date:T',
    y='temp_max:Q',
    y2='temp_min:Q',
    tooltip=['date:T', 'temp_max:Q', 'temp_min:Q']
).properties(
    width=600,
    height=300,
    title='Seattle Temperature Range'
)

# 3. Bar chart showing average temperature by month
monthly_temp = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_bar().encode(
    x='month(date):O',
    y='mean(temp_max):Q',
    color='month(date):N',
    tooltip=['month(date):O', 'mean(temp_max):Q']
).properties(
    width=600,
    height=300,
    title='Average Maximum Temperature by Month'
)

# 4. Scatter plot of precipitation vs temperature
precip_temp = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_circle(size=60).encode(
    x='temp_max:Q',
    y='precipitation:Q',
    color='weather:N',
    tooltip=['date:T', 'temp_max:Q', 'precipitation:Q', 'weather:N']
).properties(
    width=600,
    height=400,
    title='Precipitation vs Temperature by Weather Type'
)

# 5. Heatmap of temperature by month and year
heatmap = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_rect().encode(
    x='month(date):O',
    y='year(date):O',
    color=alt.Color('mean(temp_max):Q', scale=alt.Scale(scheme='viridis')),
    tooltip=['year(date):O', 'month(date):O', 'mean(temp_max):Q']
).properties(
    width=600,
    height=400,
    title='Average Maximum Temperature Heatmap'
)

# 6. Multi-panel chart showing different weather metrics
base = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).properties(width=600, height=100)

temp_panel = base.mark_line(color='red').encode(
    x='date:T',
    y=alt.Y('temp_max:Q', title='Temperature (°C)')
)

precip_panel = base.mark_bar(color='blue').encode(
    x='date:T',
    y=alt.Y('precipitation:Q', title='Precipitation (mm)')
)

wind_panel = base.mark_line(color='green').encode(
    x='date:T',
    y=alt.Y('wind:Q', title='Wind Speed')
)

multi_panel = alt.vconcat(
    temp_panel,
    precip_panel,
    wind_panel
).properties(title='Seattle Weather Metrics Over Time')

# 7. Interactive chart with selection
brush = alt.selection_interval(encodings=['x'])

upper = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_line().encode(
    x='date:T',
    y='temp_max:Q',
    color=alt.condition(brush, alt.value('steelblue'), alt.value('lightgray'))
).properties(width=600, height=200).add_params(brush)

lower = alt.Chart(seattle_weather).mark_area().encode(
    x='date:T',
    y='precipitation:Q'
).properties(width=600, height=100)

interactive_chart = alt.vconcat(upper, lower).properties(
    title='Interactive Temperature and Precipitation Chart'
)

# Display any of the charts
temp_chart  # Or any other chart variable
```

To use this code:

1. Make sure you have the required packages installed:
```bash
pip install altair vega_datasets
```

2. The dataset is automatically loaded from vega_datasets, so you don't need to download it separately.

3. Each chart can be displayed by calling the variable name in a Jupyter notebook or by using:
```python
chart.show()  # Opens in browser
# or
chart.save('filename.html')  # Saves to file
```

The code includes various visualization types:
- Line charts for temperature trends
- Area charts for temperature ranges
- Bar charts for monthly averages
- Scatter plots for relationships between variables
- Heatmaps for temporal patterns
- Multi-panel charts for multiple metrics
- Interactive charts with brushing/selection

You can modify the encodings, colors, and properties to customize the visualizations further.
